opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling laws matter for vision, but I'd frame it a bit differently from how people usually talk about it in language.

In language, the story is clean. You have next-token prediction, a huge corpus of text written by humans, and when you scale data, parameters, and compute together, the loss goes down predictably and capabilities emerge. Text is already a compressed, symbolic representation of human knowledge, so the objective is tightly aligned with what you care about.

Vision doesn't have that luxury. Pixels are high-dimensional, redundant, and noisy. Predicting the next pixel or patch doesn't obviously lead to understanding the world. So when we ask whether vision has a scaling law, the deeper question is: scaling *what*? What's the right objective, the right representation, the right data? If you scale the wrong thing, you get a beautiful curve that doesn't lead anywhere interesting.

For a long time, vision kind of borrowed its success from supervision. ImageNet labels, then CLIP-style language supervision. That works, but it means the visual representation is shaped by language. A lot of what's in an image, like spatial structure, geometry, physics, fine-grained detail, isn't captured well by captions. When you plug these encoders into multimodal LLMs, you see the weaknesses: models struggle with counting, spatial relationships, simple visual comparisons. That suggests we haven't really scaled vision itself. We've scaled language and attached vision to it.

So I think we need scaling laws in vision, but we haven't found the right axis yet. Some directions I find promising: self-supervised learning that scales without relying on language, generative models that learn about the world by trying to produce it, and video and spatial data where the model has to understand 3D structure and dynamics rather than just recognize objects. If vision is going to be a foundation for intelligence that operates in the physical world, the scaling has to come from the visual signal itself.

There's also a philosophical point. Animals had sophisticated vision long before language. Visual intelligence isn't a subset of language intelligence; in some ways it comes first. If we only treat vision as an input module for LLMs, we're probably missing something fundamental. So yes, scaling matters, but I care more about finding the right thing to scale than just making the models bigger.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling laws matter for vision and argues that the right thing to scale remains unknown; it does not advance the view that vision may not need a scaling law.

fable-5.1.text:
I think scaling laws in vision are real, but they've been harder to pin down than in language, and that difference is actually the interesting part.

In language, the setup is clean. You have one objective, next-token prediction, you have essentially unlimited text, and the loss curves line up almost suspiciously well as you scale data, compute, and parameters. Vision never had that single unifying objective. For a long time the field scaled on ImageNet classification, and we did see something like scaling behavior there, but the signal you're scaling is a thousand human-defined labels. That caps how far it can take you. So people tried self-supervised approaches, contrastive learning, masked image modeling, and each of those gave you a different curve, often with different saturation points.

What I've come to believe is that the question isn't really "do we need scaling laws in vision." We need them, because without a predictable relationship between resources and capability you can't make engineering decisions, you can't justify a training run, you're just guessing. The real question is which quantity you should be measuring. Pixels are a terrible unit. A huge fraction of the information in an image is redundant, so simply counting images or counting tokens the way you count words doesn't tell you how much actual signal the model is absorbing.

That pushes you toward thinking about scaling in terms of representation quality rather than raw loss. And this is where architecture matters more than people sometimes admit. With ConvNeXt the point we wanted to make was that the architecture, the ConvNet versus Transformer debate, was less decisive than the training recipe and the scale. Both families scale if you let them. But the choice of architecture does change the slope of the curve and how data-efficient you are, and that matters when data is the bottleneck.

The other thing I'd say is that vision is increasingly not a standalone problem. Once you put a vision encoder into a multimodal model, the scaling story becomes a joint one. The language model supplies a lot of the semantics, and what you need from the visual side shifts. Suddenly the question is how to scale visual representations so they're useful to a reasoning system, not just so they score well on a classification benchmark. I think a lot of the most important scaling work in vision in the next few years will happen in that setting, and in generative models, where the objective is dense and self-supervised in a way that looks a lot more like language.

So, short version: yes, we need them, but we should be honest that we're still figuring out what the right axes are. Treating vision as "language models but with pixels" is going to mislead you.

r001.rationale: The response argues that vision does need scaling laws, while noting that the right quantities and axes are still being worked out. It does not advance the view that vision may not need a scaling law.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling laws are very important for computer vision, but we need to be precise about what we want to scale and what we want to measure. Are we talking about image classification accuracy, or are we talking about learning a representation that can support many different tasks? Those are different goals.

If you look only at performance on a fixed benchmark, you might see diminishing returns and conclude that scaling doesn’t work anymore. But that could also mean the benchmark is no longer measuring the capabilities we care about. A model might become more useful for transfer, for example, without showing a dramatic improvement on that one metric.

So the value of a scaling law is that it makes these questions more systematic. Given more compute, should we invest in a larger model, more data, or longer training? And how does the answer change with the learning objective? We want to understand those relationships instead of making every decision through trial and error.

But I wouldn’t assume that vision has to follow exactly the same recipe as language. We need to identify the right objectives and evaluations, then establish empirically where scaling helps and where it stops helping. To me, that’s the interesting part: making progress predictable while still asking whether we’re measuring the right kind of progress.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling laws are “very important” for computer vision and argues for establishing empirically where scaling helps. It does not advance the view that vision may not need a scaling law.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling laws are really useful in computer vision, but we need to be clear about what we want to scale and what we want to measure. Is it model size, the amount of data, or training compute? And are we measuring image classification accuracy, or the quality of a representation that can transfer to many different tasks? Those choices can lead to very different conclusions.

One challenge is that you can saturate a particular benchmark before you saturate the model’s ability to learn useful visual representations. If you only look at that benchmark, you might conclude that scaling no longer helps. But maybe your evaluation just isn’t capturing the improvement.

So what I would like from a scaling law is some predictability. Before spending a huge amount of compute, can we understand whether we should train a larger model, get more diverse data, or train longer? That would make research much more efficient. At the same time, I wouldn’t treat a scaling law as a substitute for finding better architectures or learning objectives. It describes how a particular recipe behaves; improving the recipe is still a fundamental part of the problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling laws as useful for guiding compute and improving research efficiency. It raises caveats about what to scale and how to evaluate it, but does not advance the view that computer vision may not need a scaling law.
